fields.object_str: CGIMail Forms for the Public Website - Developer Documentation

content.body:
[{"type": "html", "value": "

The basic architecture

The CGIMail form widget provides an interface to CGIMail on all StandardPages on the Library public website. The module is composed of a Wagtail back-end and React front-end. You can read a brief overview of how React is integrated with Wagtail on the Library website, in the Wiki on GitHub. Generally data flows through the app in the following manner:

  1. A JSON representation of the form, a form submission success message, the CGIMail URL and URL to an API for catalog item information are all passed from the Wagtail back-end to the templates in a normal fashion through a context variable in the StandardPage model. Both the form JSON and the form submission success message are model fields propagated from the Widgets tab on StandardPages. The URLs are set in the base.py settings file. All of these data points are stored in data-attributes on a div in the base/templates/base/public_base.html template.
  2. React is injected into the template using django-webpack-loader if CGIMail form JSON is present. This is done with the render_bundle 'CGIMailForm' call in the template (bundles, e.g. CGIMailForm, are configured in the entry section of webpack.config.js).
  3. React parses the data-attributes on the div and builds the form accordingly. The final form is rendered on the page by React.

JSON

The meat of this application is the JSON object that we add to the Cgi mail form field in the CGIMail Form Widget on a StandardPage (shown below).

Simple example

In order for a CGIMail form to appear, JSON of a specific form must be provided. This JSON can be thought of as a set of instructions that our React front-end needs in order to build itself. JSON for a very simple form might look like this:

{
  "form": {
    "id": "online-help",
    "sections": [
      {
        "title": "",
        "hidden": true,
        "elements": [
          {
            "type": "hidden",
            "value": "bbusenius",
            "name": "rcpt"
          },
          {
            "type": "hidden",
            "value": "Request Help Finding an Online Copy",
            "name": "subject"
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "title": "Catalog Information",
        "elements": [
          {
            "type": "text",
            "id": "author",
            "name": "Author:",
            "required": false,
            "label": "Author",
            "map": {
              "src": "itemServlet",
              "fields": "author"
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Though this might look complicated at a glance, closer inspection will reveal that the JSON above is really just the representation of a form distilled down to only the pure data elements. The above JSON would render a form that looks like the one below. It has two sections within the form. The first section is hidden and it contains a hidden rcpt field and a hidden subject field. The second section is visible and comprises what we actually see below; an h2 that says, "Catalog Information", an author input and author label.

The simple example above demonstrates a few things about the required format of the JSON. Though not everything above is required, much of it is. The JSON must start out with a form property and it must have a sections property (containing an array) within. The first object in the sections array must have a property of hidden and the value of the hidden property must be true. Likewise, within the first object in the sections array, there must be an elements property (containing an array) and the first object here must be have a name of rcpt, a type of hidden and a value that maps to a CGIMail surrogate. All of these required properties can be found in the file: base/static/base/js/CGIMailFormSchema.js which is responsible for enforcing the format of the JSON.

Form level object properties

The following JSON properties reside at the form level in the JSON.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
id No String Adds an id to the form tag
hasRequiredFields No Bool Renders a paragraph tag with the message, "Required fields are followed by *" above the form. Should be used if the form contains required fields
hasSpringsharePP No Bool Renders a paragraph tag with the message, "This form is powered by Springshare and complies with its privacy policy.", where the words, "privacy policy" link to Springshare's policy on their site.
sections Yes Array Will render section elements with in the form based on what's contained within this array

Section level object properties

At the section level of the form JSON, the following properties are available.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
title No String Renders an h2 element within the form section with the text set here. Should be empty if the form is hidden
description No String Renders a paragraph under the section title.
hidden No Bool If set to true, the form section will be considered a hidden section and will not be visible on the page. Note: even though this property is not required for every section, every CGIMail form is expected to have a first section with this property set to true and this is enforced by the schema. This is because every CGIMail form must have a rcpt field and these are always hidden. All hidden CGIMail inputs should be configured in the first hidden section as a best practice
hiddenButVisible No Bool When set to true, displays form fields as a read-only definition list (dl/dt/dd elements) with catalog data, while still including hidden inputs for form submission. Empty fields are automatically filtered
out. The section will not be displayed if all fields are empty.
elements Yes (without these, your form won't have any fields) Array Renders inputs, select boxes, textareas, checkboxes and radio buttons based on what's inside this array

Elements

Normal elements are represented by JSON objects withing the elements array found within form sections. Each blurb of JSON representing an element, will be translated to an HTML element by the React front-end. The following is an example of an element.

{
  "type": "text",
   "id": "name",
   "name": "Reporter-",
   "required": true,
   "label": "Name",
   "placeholder": "Jean-Luc Picard",
   "map": {
     "src": "GET",
     "fields": "cn"
   }
}

The above JSON element would render an HTML <input> with an id of "name" and a name of "Reporter-". It would have a red * next to it and would be a required field with placeholder text of, "Jean-Luc Picard". It would also pre-populate with any value from the cn GET parameter if one happens to exist. The HTML would look like the HTML below. The main takeaway here is that the JSON above is transformed into the HTML below.

<div class="form-group">
  <label for="Reporter-">
    Name <abbr title="required">*</abbr>
  </label>
  <input id="Reporter-" type="text" name="Reporter-" placeholder="Jean-Luc Picard" required="" class="form-control" value=""/>
</div>

Possible element properties

Element objects can have the following properties. Though most of these are not specifically required, a form element will not render if certain properties are missing. These are marked by *.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
type No* String, must be either text, email, hidden, select, textarea, checkbox or radio This is what populates the type attribute of the HTML input and renders the corresponding HTML control
id No String Populates the id attribute on the input
name No* String Populates the name attribute of the input
required No Bool Adds the required attribute to the form input and renders a red * in an abbr element in the form label
label No String Adds a label element, will contain an abbr with an * if required is also set. If the provided string contains HTML, e.g. a link, it will be rendered within the form label (HTML must be properly escaped for JSON).
placeholder No String Populates the placeholder attribute of the input. Not applicable to elements of type hidden, select, checkbox or radio
helpText No Object with id and text properties. The id populated here will be used to populate the aria-describedby property and the text value will be the help text displayed under the form field. Both of these should be strings. Renders an aria-described by property on the field and adds an HTML small tag to display as help text underneath it. The small tag renders with a css class of form-text and an id that matches the value of the aria tag.
map No Object with src and fields properties where src is either GET or itemServlet and fields is the name or a field to map to (read more below) Maps the field to a data source and prepopulates it with a value. Currently supported data sources are GET parameters and the itemServlet (read more below)
value No String Sets the value attribute of the input if set. This will prepopulate the input with the static value
disabled No Bool Sets the initial disabled state of the element. Disabled elements appear grayed out and cannot be modified by users.
enabledWhen No Object with field and value properties (both strings) Conditionally enables the element when the specified field has the specified value. Example: {"field": "status", "value": "Available"}
disabledWhen No Object with field and value properties (both strings) Conditionally disables the element when the specified field has the specified value. Example: {"field": "status", "value": "Unavailable"}

Special elements

In addition to the normal JSON code blurbs that create inputs and other form fields, this module has two that are slightly different. These are fieldsets and groups. Just like JSON for normal form controls (like the ones listed in the table above), these are put in the elements array of the JSON. Their structure, however, is just a little different.

Fieldsets

In order to make a fieldset you will need to put JSON similar to the following in the elements array of the form section JSON:

{
  "fieldset": {
    "legend": "Location information",
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "call_number",
        "name": "Call_Number",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Call Number"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "location",
        "name": "Location-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Location"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Note the above JSON starts with a fieldset property which is just JSON code with a legend property and another elements array. The legend property just takes a string that will be used to generate the fieldset's legend. The elements array of the fieldset can be populated with JSON corresponding to normal form controls such as those listed in the table above. The only difference between these elements and the "normal" ones, is that these will be wrapped in a fieldset. The above JSON would render the following HTML:

<fieldset>
  <legend>Location information</legend>
  <div class="form-group">
    <label for="Call_Number">Call Number</label>
    <input id="Call_Number" type="text" name="Call_Number" class="form-control" value=" ">
  </div>
  <div class="form-group">
    <label for="Location-">Location</label>
    <input id="Location-" type="text" name="Location-" class="form-control" value="">
  </div>
</fieldset>

Groups

A group is almost the same as a fieldset in terms of how it is setup. The main difference is that a group just groups things visually. This is normally used when you want to display form elements horizontally.

In order to get something like this, you just need to put some JSON code with a group property and elements array in the form section elements array. Just like with the fieldset, all of the elements in the group's element array will be wrapped together. In this case, they'll be wrapped in the same div with a bootstrap form-group row and columns.

{
  "group": {
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "isbn",
        "name": "ISBN-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "ISBN"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "issn",
        "name": "ISSN-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "ISSN"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "bib_num",
        "name": "Bib_Number",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Bib number"
      }
    ]
  }
},

The above JSON would render the following HTML:

<div class="form-group row">
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="ISBN-">ISBN</label>
      <input id="ISBN-" type="text" name="ISBN-" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="ISSN-">ISSN</label>
      <input id="ISSN-" type="text" name="ISSN-" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="Bib_Number">Bib number</label>
      <input id="Bib_Number" type="text" name="Bib_Number" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

Labels

Form labels aren't really too special, however, it's worth noting that properly escaped JSON can be provided instead of a simple string. This is normally used to add a descriptive link to a label. When this is done properly (escaped), the expected HTML will render within the label instead of simple text:

{
  "type": "text",
  "id": "02_Barcode",
  "name": "02_Barcode",
  "required": true,
  "label": "Library barcode (<a href=\"https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/borrow/access-privileges/library-cards-and-account-information/\"><em>what's this</em></a>?)"
}

The above JSON would render the following label and input:

<div class="form-group">
  <label for="02_Barcode">Library barcode  (<a href="https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/borrow/access-privileges/library-cards-and-account-information/" data-ga-tracked="on"><em>what's this</em></a>?) 
    <abbr title="required">*</abbr>
  </label>
  <input id="02_Barcode" type="text" name="02_Barcode" required="" class="form-control" value="">
</div>

Conditional Fields

You can create form elements that are dynamically enabled or disabled based on the values of other form fields. This is useful for creating multi-step forms or forms where certain fields should only be available under specific conditions.

Conditional logic can be applied to individual elements, groups, or entire fieldsets using the enabledWhen or disabledWhen properties. When an element is disabled conditionally, it is rendered with reduced opacity, grayed-out appearance, and is not required (even if the required property is set to true).

Example:

{
  "fieldset": {
    "legend": "Additional Information",
    "enabledWhen": {
      "field": "request_type",
      "value": "alternative_text"
    },
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "textarea",
        "id": "description",
        "name": "Description"
        "label": "Please describe what you need",
        "required": true
      }
    ]
  }
}

In the above example, the entire fieldset will be disabled until the request_type field has a value of "alternative_text".

Note: Array GET parameters with [] notation (e.g., formats[]=Print&formats[]=Book) are automatically handled and will be joined with commas when mapped to form fields.

Mapping form fields to data sources to prepopulate forms

If you want to prepopulate a form field statically you can just use the element value property, however, in some cases you will want to prepopulate a form with values based on the GET parameter values in a URL string or another data source. This is done with the element map property. Currently we support two data sources, URL GET parameters and the itemServlet for catalog information. More data sources could easily be added in the future.

Prepopulating with GET parameters

In order to map a form input to a GET parameter just add the map property to the element JSON like below (also shown in the JSON above). It will look something like this:

"map": {
  "src": "GET",
  "fields": "cn"
}

The above element JSON will map the given input to the cn GET parameter. Thus if the visiting URL to the form is, /example-form-page/?cn="Foo+Bar", the form attached to the JSON above will be prepopulated with, "Foo Bar".

Prepopulating with the itemServlet

The itemServlet is a service that retrieves item and bibliographic information for items in the catalog. It's built into the Library website and can be accessed with a URL such as this one https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/item-servlet/?p=true&bib=6628466&barcode=103985739. It will return JSON like this:

{
  "title": "2001 a space odyssey",
  "location": "Regenstein, 2nd and 3rd Floor Video\\/DVD Collection",
  "internalLocation": "Regenstein",
  "callNumber": "PN1997.2.T97 2007",
  "callNumberPrefix": "DVD",
  "copyNumber": "c.2",
  "volumeNumber": "",
  "author": "Dullea, Keir 1936-",
  "bibId": "6628466",
  "barcode": "103985739",
  "publisher": "Warner Home Video",
  "placePublished": "United States]",
  "dateIssued": "2007",
  "edition": "Special ed. ; Widescreen ed.",
  "issn": null,
  "isbn": [
    "1419830589",
    "9781419830587"
  ]
}

In mapping inputs to the itemServlet, you do not need to worry about making a call to the itemServlet. The URL is set in the base.py settings file and Wagtail and the React front-end already know about its existence. In order to map a field to data in the itemServlet, you will need to be sure you pass the bib number and/or barcode to the form page (best to pass both if you can) as part of the URL like so: /example-form-page/?bib=6628466&barcode=103985739. If these special GET parameters are present in the form page URL and the map property src attribute is set to itemServlet, the React front-end will know to access the itemServlet and retrieve bibliographic/item information. It will map this data to your form field based on what you put in the map property. For example, the following mapping would map the title value (2001 a space odyssey) from the above itemServlet JSON to the element input where it is used:

"map": {
  "src": "itemServlet",
  "fields": "title"
}

Note: the mapping value of the fields property does not need to be a string. An array of strings will map the values of multiple itemServlet keys to a given input. For example, the following JSON would map the itemServlet placePublished and the publisher to the same input value:

"map": {
  "src": "itemServlet",
  "fields": [
    "placePublished",
    "publisher"
  ]
}

Handling array parameters:

The system automatically handles both single-value and array-style URL parameters. For example, if you have /?formats[]=Print&formats[]=Book in the URL, mapping to the formats field will automatically concatenate these values as "Print, Book".

Empty values are automatically filtered out when mapping multiple fields.

Troubleshooting

Error screen

In some cases a screen will display with a message like this:

If you see this screen, it means that the JSON entered in Wagtail does not conform to the schema in base/static/base/js/CGIMailFormSchema.js. It's most likely that you're missing a required field or a property value is set incorrectly. Note: if your JSON is invalid, this message will not appear. It only appears if your schema is incorrect. To ensure that your JSON is valid, it is always a good idea to use a JSON validation tool. There are many of them online and most of them work quite well. Always make sure your JSON validates before saving your page.

Unfortunately, error messages related to a problem with the schema are quite cryptic. What you need to understand is that they are always in reference to a specific JSON property. The example above is pointing out a problem with value of the hidden property of the very first object in form > sections. Though the message states, "must be an enum value", a quick look at CGIMailFormSchema.js tells us that the value of this property must be true.

fields.object_str: Rebecca the AI CGIMail Form editor

content.intro: Rebecca helps you create CGIMail forms using AI. Describe the form fields you need in plain language, and the tool will generate the JSON configuration for you. You can create new forms or edit existing ones. The live preview shows exactly how your form will look, and you can copy the generated JSON to use in your CGIMail form widgets where you need them.
content.title: Rebecca the AI CGIMail Form editor
content.draft_title: Rebecca the AI CGIMail Form editor
content.system_prompt:
You are an expert at generating CGIMail form JSON configurations for the University of Chicago Library website.

Your task is to generate valid JSON that follows the CGIMailFormSchema exactly. Output ONLY valid JSON with no explanations or markdown.

Key requirements:
1. The first section must always be hidden with a 'rcpt' field containing the recipient surrogate.
   These should never be email addresses. Surrogates are just text. Do not convert them into email
   addresses.
2. Use appropriate field types: text, email, textarea, select, checkbox, radio, hidden.
3. Group related fields using fieldset (with legend) or group (side-by-side).
4. Add helpful placeholder text and help text where appropriate.
5. Mark required fields with required: true.
6. Select boxes: Options for these are not lists of strings. They are lists of objects that have
   value and text attributes. Always give these a default "unselected" state.
7. Conditional fields: Use enabledWhen to show a field only when another field has a specific value.
   - enabledWhen.field must match the controlling field's name attribute (not id)
   - enabledWhen.value must exactly match one of the controlling field's option values
   Example: To show "Select your year" only for undergraduates:
   First field:  {"name": "UChicago_Affiliation", "options": [{"value": "", "text": "-- Select --", "disabled": true, "selected": true}, {"value": "Undergraduate student", ...}]}
   Second field: {"name": "Year", "enabledWhen": {"field": "UChicago_Affiliation", "value": "Undergraduate student"}}

Create an appointment request form with:
- Name (required)
- Email address (required)
- UChicago affiliation dropdown (Undergraduate student, Graduate student, Faculty or instructor, Staff, Alumni, Visitor / Not UChicago)
- If undergraduate, year dropdown (1st Year, 2nd Year, 3rd Year, Senior)
- Major, department, or program text field
- Research question summary (required, large text area)
- Is this for a UChicago course? dropdown (Yes, No)
- If yes, course name and number text field
- Research done so far (large text area)
- Accommodation notes (large text area)

content.body:
[{"type": "html", "value": "

The basic architecture

The CGIMail form widget provides an interface to CGIMail on all StandardPages on the Library public website. The module is composed of a Wagtail back-end and React front-end. You can read a brief overview of how React is integrated with Wagtail on the Library website, in the Wiki on GitHub. Generally data flows through the app in the following manner:

  1. A JSON representation of the form, a form submission success message, the CGIMail URL and URL to an API for catalog item information are all passed from the Wagtail back-end to the templates in a normal fashion through a context variable in the StandardPage model. Both the form JSON and the form submission success message are model fields propagated from the Widgets tab on StandardPages. The URLs are set in the base.py settings file. All of these data points are stored in data-attributes on a div in the base/templates/base/public_base.html template.
  2. React is injected into the template using django-webpack-loader if CGIMail form JSON is present. This is done with the render_bundle 'CGIMailForm' call in the template (bundles, e.g. CGIMailForm, are configured in the entry section of webpack.config.js).
  3. React parses the data-attributes on the div and builds the form accordingly. The final form is rendered on the page by React.

JSON

The meat of this application is the JSON object that we add to the Cgi mail form field in the CGIMail Form Widget on a StandardPage (shown below).

Simple example

In order for a CGIMail form to appear, JSON of a specific form must be provided. This JSON can be thought of as a set of instructions that our React front-end needs in order to build itself. JSON for a very simple form might look like this:

{
  "form": {
    "id": "online-help",
    "sections": [
      {
        "title": "",
        "hidden": true,
        "elements": [
          {
            "type": "hidden",
            "value": "bbusenius",
            "name": "rcpt"
          },
          {
            "type": "hidden",
            "value": "Request Help Finding an Online Copy",
            "name": "subject"
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "title": "Catalog Information",
        "elements": [
          {
            "type": "text",
            "id": "author",
            "name": "Author:",
            "required": false,
            "label": "Author",
            "map": {
              "src": "itemServlet",
              "fields": "author"
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Though this might look complicated at a glance, closer inspection will reveal that the JSON above is really just the representation of a form distilled down to only the pure data elements. The above JSON would render a form that looks like the one below. It has two sections within the form. The first section is hidden and it contains a hidden rcpt field and a hidden subject field. The second section is visible and comprises what we actually see below; an h2 that says, "Catalog Information", an author input and author label.

The simple example above demonstrates a few things about the required format of the JSON. Though not everything above is required, much of it is. The JSON must start out with a form property and it must have a sections property (containing an array) within. The first object in the sections array must have a property of hidden and the value of the hidden property must be true. Likewise, within the first object in the sections array, there must be an elements property (containing an array) and the first object here must be have a name of rcpt, a type of hidden and a value that maps to a CGIMail surrogate. All of these required properties can be found in the file: base/static/base/js/CGIMailFormSchema.js which is responsible for enforcing the format of the JSON.

Form level object properties

The following JSON properties reside at the form level in the JSON.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
id No String Adds an id to the form tag
hasRequiredFields No Bool Renders a paragraph tag with the message, "Required fields are followed by *" above the form. Should be used if the form contains required fields
hasSpringsharePP No Bool Renders a paragraph tag with the message, "This form is powered by Springshare and complies with its privacy policy.", where the words, "privacy policy" link to Springshare's policy on their site.
sections Yes Array Will render section elements with in the form based on what's contained within this array

Section level object properties

At the section level of the form JSON, the following properties are available.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
title No String Renders an h2 element within the form section with the text set here. Should be empty if the form is hidden
description No String Renders a paragraph under the section title.
hidden No Bool If set to true, the form section will be considered a hidden section and will not be visible on the page. Note: even though this property is not required for every section, every CGIMail form is expected to have a first section with this property set to true and this is enforced by the schema. This is because every CGIMail form must have a rcpt field and these are always hidden. All hidden CGIMail inputs should be configured in the first hidden section as a best practice
hiddenButVisible No Bool When set to true, displays form fields as a read-only definition list (dl/dt/dd elements) with catalog data, while still including hidden inputs for form submission. Empty fields are automatically filtered
out. The section will not be displayed if all fields are empty.
elements Yes (without these, your form won't have any fields) Array Renders inputs, select boxes, textareas, checkboxes and radio buttons based on what's inside this array

Elements

Normal elements are represented by JSON objects withing the elements array found within form sections. Each blurb of JSON representing an element, will be translated to an HTML element by the React front-end. The following is an example of an element.

{
  "type": "text",
   "id": "name",
   "name": "Reporter-",
   "required": true,
   "label": "Name",
   "placeholder": "Jean-Luc Picard",
   "map": {
     "src": "GET",
     "fields": "cn"
   }
}

The above JSON element would render an HTML <input> with an id of "name" and a name of "Reporter-". It would have a red * next to it and would be a required field with placeholder text of, "Jean-Luc Picard". It would also pre-populate with any value from the cn GET parameter if one happens to exist. The HTML would look like the HTML below. The main takeaway here is that the JSON above is transformed into the HTML below.

<div class="form-group">
  <label for="Reporter-">
    Name <abbr title="required">*</abbr>
  </label>
  <input id="Reporter-" type="text" name="Reporter-" placeholder="Jean-Luc Picard" required="" class="form-control" value=""/>
</div>

Possible element properties

Element objects can have the following properties. Though most of these are not specifically required, a form element will not render if certain properties are missing. These are marked by *.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
type No* String, must be either text, email, hidden, select, textarea, checkbox or radio This is what populates the type attribute of the HTML input and renders the corresponding HTML control
id No String Populates the id attribute on the input
name No* String Populates the name attribute of the input
required No Bool Adds the required attribute to the form input and renders a red * in an abbr element in the form label
label No String Adds a label element, will contain an abbr with an * if required is also set. If the provided string contains HTML, e.g. a link, it will be rendered within the form label (HTML must be properly escaped for JSON).
placeholder No String Populates the placeholder attribute of the input. Not applicable to elements of type hidden, select, checkbox or radio
helpText No Object with id and text properties. The id populated here will be used to populate the aria-describedby property and the text value will be the help text displayed under the form field. Both of these should be strings. Renders an aria-described by property on the field and adds an HTML small tag to display as help text underneath it. The small tag renders with a css class of form-text and an id that matches the value of the aria tag.
map No Object with src and fields properties where src is either GET or itemServlet and fields is the name or a field to map to (read more below) Maps the field to a data source and prepopulates it with a value. Currently supported data sources are GET parameters and the itemServlet (read more below)
value No String Sets the value attribute of the input if set. This will prepopulate the input with the static value
disabled No Bool Sets the initial disabled state of the element. Disabled elements appear grayed out and cannot be modified by users.
enabledWhen No Object with field and value properties (both strings) Conditionally enables the element when the specified field has the specified value. Example: {"field": "status", "value": "Available"}
disabledWhen No Object with field and value properties (both strings) Conditionally disables the element when the specified field has the specified value. Example: {"field": "status", "value": "Unavailable"}

Special elements

In addition to the normal JSON code blurbs that create inputs and other form fields, this module has two that are slightly different. These are fieldsets and groups. Just like JSON for normal form controls (like the ones listed in the table above), these are put in the elements array of the JSON. Their structure, however, is just a little different.

Fieldsets

In order to make a fieldset you will need to put JSON similar to the following in the elements array of the form section JSON:

{
  "fieldset": {
    "legend": "Location information",
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "call_number",
        "name": "Call_Number",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Call Number"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "location",
        "name": "Location-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Location"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Note the above JSON starts with a fieldset property which is just JSON code with a legend property and another elements array. The legend property just takes a string that will be used to generate the fieldset's legend. The elements array of the fieldset can be populated with JSON corresponding to normal form controls such as those listed in the table above. The only difference between these elements and the "normal" ones, is that these will be wrapped in a fieldset. The above JSON would render the following HTML:

<fieldset>
  <legend>Location information</legend>
  <div class="form-group">
    <label for="Call_Number">Call Number</label>
    <input id="Call_Number" type="text" name="Call_Number" class="form-control" value=" ">
  </div>
  <div class="form-group">
    <label for="Location-">Location</label>
    <input id="Location-" type="text" name="Location-" class="form-control" value="">
  </div>
</fieldset>

Groups

A group is almost the same as a fieldset in terms of how it is setup. The main difference is that a group just groups things visually. This is normally used when you want to display form elements horizontally.

In order to get something like this, you just need to put some JSON code with a group property and elements array in the form section elements array. Just like with the fieldset, all of the elements in the group's element array will be wrapped together. In this case, they'll be wrapped in the same div with a bootstrap form-group row and columns.

{
  "group": {
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "isbn",
        "name": "ISBN-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "ISBN"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "issn",
        "name": "ISSN-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "ISSN"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "bib_num",
        "name": "Bib_Number",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Bib number"
      }
    ]
  }
},

The above JSON would render the following HTML:

<div class="form-group row">
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="ISBN-">ISBN</label>
      <input id="ISBN-" type="text" name="ISBN-" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="ISSN-">ISSN</label>
      <input id="ISSN-" type="text" name="ISSN-" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="Bib_Number">Bib number</label>
      <input id="Bib_Number" type="text" name="Bib_Number" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

Labels

Form labels aren't really too special, however, it's worth noting that properly escaped JSON can be provided instead of a simple string. This is normally used to add a descriptive link to a label. When this is done properly (escaped), the expected HTML will render within the label instead of simple text:

{
  "type": "text",
  "id": "02_Barcode",
  "name": "02_Barcode",
  "required": true,
  "label": "Library barcode (<a href=\"https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/borrow/access-privileges/library-cards-and-account-information/\"><em>what's this</em></a>?)"
}

The above JSON would render the following label and input:

<div class="form-group">
  <label for="02_Barcode">Library barcode  (<a href="https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/borrow/access-privileges/library-cards-and-account-information/" data-ga-tracked="on"><em>what's this</em></a>?) 
    <abbr title="required">*</abbr>
  </label>
  <input id="02_Barcode" type="text" name="02_Barcode" required="" class="form-control" value="">
</div>

Conditional Fields

You can create form elements that are dynamically enabled or disabled based on the values of other form fields. This is useful for creating multi-step forms or forms where certain fields should only be available under specific conditions.

Conditional logic can be applied to individual elements, groups, or entire fieldsets using the enabledWhen or disabledWhen properties. When an element is disabled conditionally, it is rendered with reduced opacity, grayed-out appearance, and is not required (even if the required property is set to true).

Example:

{
  "fieldset": {
    "legend": "Additional Information",
    "enabledWhen": {
      "field": "request_type",
      "value": "alternative_text"
    },
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "textarea",
        "id": "description",
        "name": "Description"
        "label": "Please describe what you need",
        "required": true
      }
    ]
  }
}

In the above example, the entire fieldset will be disabled until the request_type field has a value of "alternative_text".

Note: Array GET parameters with [] notation (e.g., formats[]=Print&formats[]=Book) are automatically handled and will be joined with commas when mapped to form fields.

Mapping form fields to data sources to prepopulate forms

If you want to prepopulate a form field statically you can just use the element value property, however, in some cases you will want to prepopulate a form with values based on the GET parameter values in a URL string or another data source. This is done with the element map property. Currently we support two data sources, URL GET parameters and the itemServlet for catalog information. More data sources could easily be added in the future.

Prepopulating with GET parameters

In order to map a form input to a GET parameter just add the map property to the element JSON like below (also shown in the JSON above). It will look something like this:

"map": {
  "src": "GET",
  "fields": "cn"
}

The above element JSON will map the given input to the cn GET parameter. Thus if the visiting URL to the form is, /example-form-page/?cn="Foo+Bar", the form attached to the JSON above will be prepopulated with, "Foo Bar".

Prepopulating with the itemServlet

The itemServlet is a service that retrieves item and bibliographic information for items in the catalog. It's built into the Library website and can be accessed with a URL such as this one https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/item-servlet/?p=true&bib=6628466&barcode=103985739. It will return JSON like this:

{
  "title": "2001 a space odyssey",
  "location": "Regenstein, 2nd and 3rd Floor Video\\/DVD Collection",
  "internalLocation": "Regenstein",
  "callNumber": "PN1997.2.T97 2007",
  "callNumberPrefix": "DVD",
  "copyNumber": "c.2",
  "volumeNumber": "",
  "author": "Dullea, Keir 1936-",
  "bibId": "6628466",
  "barcode": "103985739",
  "publisher": "Warner Home Video",
  "placePublished": "United States]",
  "dateIssued": "2007",
  "edition": "Special ed. ; Widescreen ed.",
  "issn": null,
  "isbn": [
    "1419830589",
    "9781419830587"
  ]
}

In mapping inputs to the itemServlet, you do not need to worry about making a call to the itemServlet. The URL is set in the base.py settings file and Wagtail and the React front-end already know about its existence. In order to map a field to data in the itemServlet, you will need to be sure you pass the bib number and/or barcode to the form page (best to pass both if you can) as part of the URL like so: /example-form-page/?bib=6628466&barcode=103985739. If these special GET parameters are present in the form page URL and the map property src attribute is set to itemServlet, the React front-end will know to access the itemServlet and retrieve bibliographic/item information. It will map this data to your form field based on what you put in the map property. For example, the following mapping would map the title value (2001 a space odyssey) from the above itemServlet JSON to the element input where it is used:

"map": {
  "src": "itemServlet",
  "fields": "title"
}

Note: the mapping value of the fields property does not need to be a string. An array of strings will map the values of multiple itemServlet keys to a given input. For example, the following JSON would map the itemServlet placePublished and the publisher to the same input value:

"map": {
  "src": "itemServlet",
  "fields": [
    "placePublished",
    "publisher"
  ]
}

Handling array parameters:

The system automatically handles both single-value and array-style URL parameters. For example, if you have /?formats[]=Print&formats[]=Book in the URL, mapping to the formats field will automatically concatenate these values as "Print, Book".

Empty values are automatically filtered out when mapping multiple fields.

Troubleshooting

Error screen

In some cases a screen will display with a message like this:

If you see this screen, it means that the JSON entered in Wagtail does not conform to the schema in base/static/base/js/CGIMailFormSchema.js. It's most likely that you're missing a required field or a property value is set incorrectly. Note: if your JSON is invalid, this message will not appear. It only appears if your schema is incorrect. To ensure that your JSON is valid, it is always a good idea to use a JSON validation tool. There are many of them online and most of them work quite well. Always make sure your JSON validates before saving your page.

Unfortunately, error messages related to a problem with the schema are quite cryptic. What you need to understand is that they are always in reference to a specific JSON property. The example above is pointing out a problem with value of the hidden property of the very first object in form > sections. Though the message states, "must be an enum value", a quick look at CGIMailFormSchema.js tells us that the value of this property must be true.

", "id": "83954373-85f6-4102-91bb-27f5fc781ef9"}]

The basic architecture

The CGIMail form widget provides an interface to CGIMail on all StandardPages on the Library public website. The module is composed of a Wagtail back-end and React front-end. You can read a brief overview of how React is integrated with Wagtail on the Library website, in the Wiki on GitHub. Generally data flows through the app in the following manner:

  1. A JSON representation of the form, a form submission success message, the CGIMail URL and URL to an API for catalog item information are all passed from the Wagtail back-end to the templates in a normal fashion through a context variable in the StandardPage model. Both the form JSON and the form submission success message are model fields propagated from the Widgets tab on StandardPages. The URLs are set in the base.py settings file. All of these data points are stored in data-attributes on a div in the base/templates/base/public_base.html template.
  2. React is injected into the template using django-webpack-loader if CGIMail form JSON is present. This is done with the render_bundle 'CGIMailForm' call in the template (bundles, e.g. CGIMailForm, are configured in the entry section of webpack.config.js).
  3. React parses the data-attributes on the div and builds the form accordingly. The final form is rendered on the page by React.

JSON

The meat of this application is the JSON object that we add to the Cgi mail form field in the CGIMail Form Widget on a StandardPage (shown below).

Simple example

In order for a CGIMail form to appear, JSON of a specific form must be provided. This JSON can be thought of as a set of instructions that our React front-end needs in order to build itself. JSON for a very simple form might look like this:

{
  "form": {
    "id": "online-help",
    "sections": [
      {
        "title": "",
        "hidden": true,
        "elements": [
          {
            "type": "hidden",
            "value": "bbusenius",
            "name": "rcpt"
          },
          {
            "type": "hidden",
            "value": "Request Help Finding an Online Copy",
            "name": "subject"
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "title": "Catalog Information",
        "elements": [
          {
            "type": "text",
            "id": "author",
            "name": "Author:",
            "required": false,
            "label": "Author",
            "map": {
              "src": "itemServlet",
              "fields": "author"
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Though this might look complicated at a glance, closer inspection will reveal that the JSON above is really just the representation of a form distilled down to only the pure data elements. The above JSON would render a form that looks like the one below. It has two sections within the form. The first section is hidden and it contains a hidden rcpt field and a hidden subject field. The second section is visible and comprises what we actually see below; an h2 that says, "Catalog Information", an author input and author label.

The simple example above demonstrates a few things about the required format of the JSON. Though not everything above is required, much of it is. The JSON must start out with a form property and it must have a sections property (containing an array) within. The first object in the sections array must have a property of hidden and the value of the hidden property must be true. Likewise, within the first object in the sections array, there must be an elements property (containing an array) and the first object here must be have a name of rcpt, a type of hidden and a value that maps to a CGIMail surrogate. All of these required properties can be found in the file: base/static/base/js/CGIMailFormSchema.js which is responsible for enforcing the format of the JSON.

Form level object properties

The following JSON properties reside at the form level in the JSON.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
id No String Adds an id to the form tag
hasRequiredFields No Bool Renders a paragraph tag with the message, "Required fields are followed by *" above the form. Should be used if the form contains required fields
hasSpringsharePP No Bool Renders a paragraph tag with the message, "This form is powered by Springshare and complies with its privacy policy.", where the words, "privacy policy" link to Springshare's policy on their site.
sections Yes Array Will render section elements with in the form based on what's contained within this array

Section level object properties

At the section level of the form JSON, the following properties are available.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
title No String Renders an h2 element within the form section with the text set here. Should be empty if the form is hidden
description No String Renders a paragraph under the section title.
hidden No Bool If set to true, the form section will be considered a hidden section and will not be visible on the page. Note: even though this property is not required for every section, every CGIMail form is expected to have a first section with this property set to true and this is enforced by the schema. This is because every CGIMail form must have a rcpt field and these are always hidden. All hidden CGIMail inputs should be configured in the first hidden section as a best practice
hiddenButVisible No Bool When set to true, displays form fields as a read-only definition list (dl/dt/dd elements) with catalog data, while still including hidden inputs for form submission. Empty fields are automatically filtered
out. The section will not be displayed if all fields are empty.
elements Yes (without these, your form won't have any fields) Array Renders inputs, select boxes, textareas, checkboxes and radio buttons based on what's inside this array

Elements

Normal elements are represented by JSON objects withing the elements array found within form sections. Each blurb of JSON representing an element, will be translated to an HTML element by the React front-end. The following is an example of an element.

{
  "type": "text",
   "id": "name",
   "name": "Reporter-",
   "required": true,
   "label": "Name",
   "placeholder": "Jean-Luc Picard",
   "map": {
     "src": "GET",
     "fields": "cn"
   }
}

The above JSON element would render an HTML <input> with an id of "name" and a name of "Reporter-". It would have a red * next to it and would be a required field with placeholder text of, "Jean-Luc Picard". It would also pre-populate with any value from the cn GET parameter if one happens to exist. The HTML would look like the HTML below. The main takeaway here is that the JSON above is transformed into the HTML below.

<div class="form-group">
  <label for="Reporter-">
    Name <abbr title="required">*</abbr>
  </label>
  <input id="Reporter-" type="text" name="Reporter-" placeholder="Jean-Luc Picard" required="" class="form-control" value=""/>
</div>

Possible element properties

Element objects can have the following properties. Though most of these are not specifically required, a form element will not render if certain properties are missing. These are marked by *.

Property Name Required Value Renders in HTML
type No* String, must be either text, email, hidden, select, textarea, checkbox or radio This is what populates the type attribute of the HTML input and renders the corresponding HTML control
id No String Populates the id attribute on the input
name No* String Populates the name attribute of the input
required No Bool Adds the required attribute to the form input and renders a red * in an abbr element in the form label
label No String Adds a label element, will contain an abbr with an * if required is also set. If the provided string contains HTML, e.g. a link, it will be rendered within the form label (HTML must be properly escaped for JSON).
placeholder No String Populates the placeholder attribute of the input. Not applicable to elements of type hidden, select, checkbox or radio
helpText No Object with id and text properties. The id populated here will be used to populate the aria-describedby property and the text value will be the help text displayed under the form field. Both of these should be strings. Renders an aria-described by property on the field and adds an HTML small tag to display as help text underneath it. The small tag renders with a css class of form-text and an id that matches the value of the aria tag.
map No Object with src and fields properties where src is either GET or itemServlet and fields is the name or a field to map to (read more below) Maps the field to a data source and prepopulates it with a value. Currently supported data sources are GET parameters and the itemServlet (read more below)
value No String Sets the value attribute of the input if set. This will prepopulate the input with the static value
disabled No Bool Sets the initial disabled state of the element. Disabled elements appear grayed out and cannot be modified by users.
enabledWhen No Object with field and value properties (both strings) Conditionally enables the element when the specified field has the specified value. Example: {"field": "status", "value": "Available"}
disabledWhen No Object with field and value properties (both strings) Conditionally disables the element when the specified field has the specified value. Example: {"field": "status", "value": "Unavailable"}

Special elements

In addition to the normal JSON code blurbs that create inputs and other form fields, this module has two that are slightly different. These are fieldsets and groups. Just like JSON for normal form controls (like the ones listed in the table above), these are put in the elements array of the JSON. Their structure, however, is just a little different.

Fieldsets

In order to make a fieldset you will need to put JSON similar to the following in the elements array of the form section JSON:

{
  "fieldset": {
    "legend": "Location information",
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "call_number",
        "name": "Call_Number",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Call Number"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "location",
        "name": "Location-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Location"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Note the above JSON starts with a fieldset property which is just JSON code with a legend property and another elements array. The legend property just takes a string that will be used to generate the fieldset's legend. The elements array of the fieldset can be populated with JSON corresponding to normal form controls such as those listed in the table above. The only difference between these elements and the "normal" ones, is that these will be wrapped in a fieldset. The above JSON would render the following HTML:

<fieldset>
  <legend>Location information</legend>
  <div class="form-group">
    <label for="Call_Number">Call Number</label>
    <input id="Call_Number" type="text" name="Call_Number" class="form-control" value=" ">
  </div>
  <div class="form-group">
    <label for="Location-">Location</label>
    <input id="Location-" type="text" name="Location-" class="form-control" value="">
  </div>
</fieldset>

Groups

A group is almost the same as a fieldset in terms of how it is setup. The main difference is that a group just groups things visually. This is normally used when you want to display form elements horizontally.

In order to get something like this, you just need to put some JSON code with a group property and elements array in the form section elements array. Just like with the fieldset, all of the elements in the group's element array will be wrapped together. In this case, they'll be wrapped in the same div with a bootstrap form-group row and columns.

{
  "group": {
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "isbn",
        "name": "ISBN-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "ISBN"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "issn",
        "name": "ISSN-",
        "required": false,
        "label": "ISSN"
      },
      {
        "type": "text",
        "id": "bib_num",
        "name": "Bib_Number",
        "required": false,
        "label": "Bib number"
      }
    ]
  }
},

The above JSON would render the following HTML:

<div class="form-group row">
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="ISBN-">ISBN</label>
      <input id="ISBN-" type="text" name="ISBN-" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="ISSN-">ISSN</label>
      <input id="ISSN-" type="text" name="ISSN-" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="col-sm-4">
    <div class="form-group">
      <label for="Bib_Number">Bib number</label>
      <input id="Bib_Number" type="text" name="Bib_Number" class="form-control" value="">
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

Labels

Form labels aren't really too special, however, it's worth noting that properly escaped JSON can be provided instead of a simple string. This is normally used to add a descriptive link to a label. When this is done properly (escaped), the expected HTML will render within the label instead of simple text:

{
  "type": "text",
  "id": "02_Barcode",
  "name": "02_Barcode",
  "required": true,
  "label": "Library barcode (<a href=\"https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/borrow/access-privileges/library-cards-and-account-information/\"><em>what's this</em></a>?)"
}

The above JSON would render the following label and input:

<div class="form-group">
  <label for="02_Barcode">Library barcode  (<a href="https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/borrow/access-privileges/library-cards-and-account-information/" data-ga-tracked="on"><em>what's this</em></a>?) 
    <abbr title="required">*</abbr>
  </label>
  <input id="02_Barcode" type="text" name="02_Barcode" required="" class="form-control" value="">
</div>

Conditional Fields

You can create form elements that are dynamically enabled or disabled based on the values of other form fields. This is useful for creating multi-step forms or forms where certain fields should only be available under specific conditions.

Conditional logic can be applied to individual elements, groups, or entire fieldsets using the enabledWhen or disabledWhen properties. When an element is disabled conditionally, it is rendered with reduced opacity, grayed-out appearance, and is not required (even if the required property is set to true).

Example:

{
  "fieldset": {
    "legend": "Additional Information",
    "enabledWhen": {
      "field": "request_type",
      "value": "alternative_text"
    },
    "elements": [
      {
        "type": "textarea",
        "id": "description",
        "name": "Description"
        "label": "Please describe what you need",
        "required": true
      }
    ]
  }
}

In the above example, the entire fieldset will be disabled until the request_type field has a value of "alternative_text".

Note: Array GET parameters with [] notation (e.g., formats[]=Print&formats[]=Book) are automatically handled and will be joined with commas when mapped to form fields.

Mapping form fields to data sources to prepopulate forms

If you want to prepopulate a form field statically you can just use the element value property, however, in some cases you will want to prepopulate a form with values based on the GET parameter values in a URL string or another data source. This is done with the element map property. Currently we support two data sources, URL GET parameters and the itemServlet for catalog information. More data sources could easily be added in the future.

Prepopulating with GET parameters

In order to map a form input to a GET parameter just add the map property to the element JSON like below (also shown in the JSON above). It will look something like this:

"map": {
  "src": "GET",
  "fields": "cn"
}

The above element JSON will map the given input to the cn GET parameter. Thus if the visiting URL to the form is, /example-form-page/?cn="Foo+Bar", the form attached to the JSON above will be prepopulated with, "Foo Bar".

Prepopulating with the itemServlet

The itemServlet is a service that retrieves item and bibliographic information for items in the catalog. It's built into the Library website and can be accessed with a URL such as this one https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/item-servlet/?p=true&bib=6628466&barcode=103985739. It will return JSON like this:

{
  "title": "2001 a space odyssey",
  "location": "Regenstein, 2nd and 3rd Floor Video\\/DVD Collection",
  "internalLocation": "Regenstein",
  "callNumber": "PN1997.2.T97 2007",
  "callNumberPrefix": "DVD",
  "copyNumber": "c.2",
  "volumeNumber": "",
  "author": "Dullea, Keir 1936-",
  "bibId": "6628466",
  "barcode": "103985739",
  "publisher": "Warner Home Video",
  "placePublished": "United States]",
  "dateIssued": "2007",
  "edition": "Special ed. ; Widescreen ed.",
  "issn": null,
  "isbn": [
    "1419830589",
    "9781419830587"
  ]
}

In mapping inputs to the itemServlet, you do not need to worry about making a call to the itemServlet. The URL is set in the base.py settings file and Wagtail and the React front-end already know about its existence. In order to map a field to data in the itemServlet, you will need to be sure you pass the bib number and/or barcode to the form page (best to pass both if you can) as part of the URL like so: /example-form-page/?bib=6628466&barcode=103985739. If these special GET parameters are present in the form page URL and the map property src attribute is set to itemServlet, the React front-end will know to access the itemServlet and retrieve bibliographic/item information. It will map this data to your form field based on what you put in the map property. For example, the following mapping would map the title value (2001 a space odyssey) from the above itemServlet JSON to the element input where it is used:

"map": {
  "src": "itemServlet",
  "fields": "title"
}

Note: the mapping value of the fields property does not need to be a string. An array of strings will map the values of multiple itemServlet keys to a given input. For example, the following JSON would map the itemServlet placePublished and the publisher to the same input value:

"map": {
  "src": "itemServlet",
  "fields": [
    "placePublished",
    "publisher"
  ]
}

Handling array parameters:

The system automatically handles both single-value and array-style URL parameters. For example, if you have /?formats[]=Print&formats[]=Book in the URL, mapping to the formats field will automatically concatenate these values as "Print, Book".

Empty values are automatically filtered out when mapping multiple fields.

Troubleshooting

Error screen

In some cases a screen will display with a message like this:

If you see this screen, it means that the JSON entered in Wagtail does not conform to the schema in base/static/base/js/CGIMailFormSchema.js. It's most likely that you're missing a required field or a property value is set incorrectly. Note: if your JSON is invalid, this message will not appear. It only appears if your schema is incorrect. To ensure that your JSON is valid, it is always a good idea to use a JSON validation tool. There are many of them online and most of them work quite well. Always make sure your JSON validates before saving your page.

Unfortunately, error messages related to a problem with the schema are quite cryptic. What you need to understand is that they are always in reference to a specific JSON property. The example above is pointing out a problem with value of the hidden property of the very first object in form > sections. Though the message states, "must be an enum value", a quick look at CGIMailFormSchema.js tells us that the value of this property must be true.

fields.system_prompt:
You are an expert at generating CGIMail form JSON configurations for the University of Chicago Library website.

Your task is to generate valid JSON that follows the CGIMailFormSchema exactly. Output ONLY valid JSON with no explanations or markdown.

Key requirements:
1. The first section must always be hidden with a 'rcpt' field containing the recipient surrogate.
   These should never be email addresses. Surrogates are just text. Do not convert them into email
   addresses.
2. Use appropriate field types: text, email, textarea, select, checkbox, radio, hidden.
3. Group related fields using fieldset (with legend) or group (side-by-side).
4. Add helpful placeholder text and help text where appropriate.
5. Mark required fields with required: true.
6. Select boxes: Options for these are not lists of strings. They are lists of objects that have
   value and text attributes. Always give these a default "unselected" state.
7. Conditional fields: Use enabledWhen to show a field only when another field has a specific value.
   - enabledWhen.field must match the controlling field's name attribute (not id)
   - enabledWhen.value must exactly match one of the controlling field's option values
   Example: To show "Select your year" only for undergraduates:
   First field:  {"name": "UChicago_Affiliation", "options": [{"value": "", "text": "-- Select --", "disabled": true, "selected": true}, {"value": "Undergraduate student", ...}]}
   Second field: {"name": "Year", "enabledWhen": {"field": "UChicago_Affiliation", "value": "Undergraduate student"}}

[{"id": "54aa64de-758b-4afa-856c-b8690fe3de93", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

"Data in libraries: the big picture,” is a satellite pre-conference to the IFLA 2016 WLIC.  

The one-day program will take place on August 10, 2016 and is hosted by the University of Chicago Library.

Presentation slides

Thanks to all of you who attended Data In Libraries: The Big Picture. Most presentation slides are now available at: 

http://www.ifla.org/academic-and-research-libraries/conferences

"}}, {"id": "d4f2d4a4-91a5-402e-a0ad-d48b1a09c1f3", "type": "h2", "value": "Registration"}, {"id": "6399ec28-6fd8-4bf5-a1bf-f59784e063ac", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

There is no fee to attend, but space is limited and pre-registration is required.

Registration closed on July 15th.

Tours of the Joe and Rika Mansueto Library will be offered concurrently with the program.  Attendees may sign up for tours on the morning of the program.

"}}, {"id": "d56693ff-3cee-4fcd-8b21-c19265dc8d79", "type": "h2", "value": "Description"}, {"id": "bdacb45e-a07d-4c22-984c-ac788f5bea17", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "The modern, digital library has moved beyond its traditional focus on metadata, bibliographic, and authority data, and now manages or works with a broad set of data types, leveraging an ever-expanding set of tools and techniques to do so.  Those new tools also mean that even traditional data logs can be analyzed to improve the services librarians and libraries offer.  

The emergence of linked data has simultaneously created a broad spectrum of new use cases for library data.  Library catalogs now incorporate links to external datasets, and integrate those datasets in new applications.  Activities like digitization, digital preservation, online resource management, web archiving, and text and data mining all create new types of data that libraries both consume and curate.  Big Data technologies like data virtualization, parallel computing, predictive analytics, and machine learning bring the promise of improved performances and smart tools.  Libraries are thus empowered to consume and curate data of all kinds in new and innovative ways.

This one-day pre-conference will attempt to bring together the worlds of big data and linked data, and examine the "big picture” of library data, and attempting to assess the promise that these technologies hold for libraries.  Specific topics for discussion will be based on responses to the call for papers, but may include:
  • consumption of library linked data along with other types of semantic data
  • curation of research data or other types of user generated data
  • innovative data technologies used for digital preservation and digital libraries
  • analysis of library data using tools such as machine learning, text and data mining or data visualization
  • marketing initiatives in libraries based on users logs and tracks analysis
"}}, {"id": "ea1b78f8-0699-4b2d-978e-3643cca129a1", "type": "h2", "value": "Who should attend?"}, {"id": "ed34fdea-ecae-454b-982c-d660244a8cdd", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

All are welcome, but we anticipate the program will be of most interest to metadata librarians, IT librarians, data scientists, academics involved in data curation projects.

"}}, {"id": "901c7772-ee23-4dd2-85da-7f369ea7f595", "type": "h2", "value": "Call for Papers"}, {"id": "419e1ab3-b55e-48e6-a179-4a5561d491a0", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

The program’s call for papers closed on 21 February 2016.  You can find detail on the call for papers on the IFLA site.

"}}]

Bus transportation on the day of the conference

Bus transportation between the Omni Chicago Hotel and the Regenstein Library will be provided at the beginning and end of the conference day. In addition, departing buses will transport interested participants to subway connections to the airport. 

Morning buses

Morning buses will arrive at the Omni at approximately 7:30 a.m., and depart for Regenstein promptly at 7:45 a.m.

Evening buses  

In the evening, two buses will depart Regenstein, each making two stops.

One bus will stop first at Roosevelt Station, where you can board the Orange line to Midway airport, before continuing on to the Omni.

The other bus will stop first at Jackson Station, where the Blue line connects to O’Hare airport, again before continuing on to the Omni. 

You can find more information on airport connections on the CTA website: http://www.transitchicago.com/airports/

Directions to campus

By mass transit

By car

Parking

Visitor Parking provides information about visitor parking options, including locations and fees for parking garages and lots. Free parking is available on the street, but can be difficult to find during the day.

"}}, {"id": "4e7e3665-9352-4f04-a0ee-e45bc8088c31", "type": "h2", "value": "Meals"}, {"id": "68776fce-15fb-44d0-9b3c-9970edce660c", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

Breakfast and lunch will be provided during the program.  Attendees will be responsible for dinner on their own.

"}}, {"id": "39707687-a985-4e01-b8c9-60e898d2a849", "type": "h2", "value": "Congress Participation Grants"}, {"id": "fb3099f5-681b-441e-ab49-6d70ceb4570e", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

A list of opportunities for support for attendance at IFLA is available on their Conference Participation Grants webpage.  Because attendance fees are already underwritten, no additional support for this pre-conference is available. 

"}}]

fields.short_abstract: Images from more than 4,500 glass lantern slides, glass negatives, and photographic prints, created by faculty members and students of the University of Chicago Department of Botany between 1891 and 1936, influential in the development of modern ecological studies. These photographs provide an overview of important representative natural landscapes across the nation
fields.full_description:
[{"id": "a9ef1cb0-a76a-4d6b-8e45-9a8c38f54963", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

The American Environmental Photographs collection consists of 4,500 photographs\u00a0documenting natural environments, ecologies, and plant communities in the\u00a0United States at the end of the nineteenth and the beginning of the twentieth\u00a0century.

The photographs in the collection were created between 1891 and 1936 by faculty\u00a0members and students in the Department of Botany of the University of Chicago.\u00a0The research and field studies of these Chicago botanists, including Henry\u00a0Chandler Cowles (1869-1939) and George Damon Fuller (1869-1961), are considered\u00a0to be among the most influential contributions to the development of modern\u00a0ecological studies.

The images in the American Environmental Photographs collection were taken on\u00a0field trips and botanical excursions across the North American continent.\u00a0These historic documentary photographs demonstrate the character of a wide\u00a0range of American topography, its forestation, aridity, shifting coastal dune\u00a0complexes, and watercourses. Comparison of early photographs with later views\u00a0of the same setting can highlight significant changes resulting from natural\u00a0alterations of the landscape, disturbances from industry and development, or\u00a0effective natural resource usage.

Digitization of the American Environmental Photographs collection was made\u00a0possible by a grant awarded to the University of Chicago by the Library of\u00a0Congress / Ameritech National Digital Library Competition in 1997. The\u00a0LC/Ameritech program enabled U.S. libraries, archives, museums, and historical\u00a0societies to digitize collections of American historical materials for\u00a0inclusion in American Memory, the Library of Congress online collection of\u00a0primary source materials in U.S. history and culture. Images from more than\u00a04,500 glass lantern slides, glass negatives, and photographic prints, created\u00a0by faculty members and students of the University of Chicago Department of\u00a0Botany between 1891 and 1936, influential in the development of modern\u00a0ecological studies. These photographs provide an overview of important\u00a0representative natural landscapes across the nation.

"}}]
fields.access_instructions: The American Environmental Photographs collection is now hosted by the University of Chicago Library and has been made part of the University of Chicago Photographic Archive as the series Botany Department.

fields.short_abstract: The AIIS collection from the Center for Art and Archaeology in Gurgaon, Haryana, India, has over 125,000 photographs in the collection. The images fall into the broad categories of architecture, sculpture, terracotta, painting and numismatics.
fields.full_description:
[{"id": "b41992bc-944c-42ed-bddb-1e384fb4d96a", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

American knowledge of India is shaped by the American Institute of Indian\u00a0Studies, a consortium of universities and colleges in the United States at\u00a0which scholars actively engage in teaching and research about India. Since\u00a01961, the Institute has provided fellowship support for scholars and PhD\u00a0candidates in America. It has offered on-site training in Indian languages\u00a0through the superb facilities of its Language Centers. And it has extended\u00a0knowledge of Indian culture through its two Research Centers. As a member of\u00a0the Council of American Overseas Research Centers (CAORC), AIIS's online photo\u00a0archive is also linked as part of CAORC's Digital Library for International\u00a0Research.

More than 5,500 scholars have received AIIS support. Their work has spanned\u00a0fields ranging from anthropology to zoology. The outcome of their work has\u00a0resulted in literally hundreds of books and thousands of articles, the basis of\u00a0America's knowledge about India. Collections of some 3,000 books directly or\u00a0indirectly resulting from AIIS-sponsored research have been given to major\u00a0libraries in India, including the Nehru Memorial Museum and Library in New\u00a0Delhi, National Library in Calcutta, the Adyar Library in Madras and the Deccan\u00a0College in Pune. The listing of these books forms the core of a widely used and\u00a0highly appreciated work by N. Gerald Barrier, India and America, published by\u00a0the Institute.

AIIS scholars also have come together with colleagues from India and often from\u00a0other countries as well at major international conferences organized by the\u00a0Institute. These conferences have resulted in the publication of selected\u00a0papers that often form the core of knowledge in many disciplines. Nearly\u00a0seventy books have so far been published directly by the Institute.

Through its programs of research and documentation, the Institute has\u00a0endeavored to achieve an accurate and probing knowledge of India's cultures,\u00a0history, languages and present-day dynamics. Through its own publications and\u00a0those of its fellows, the Institute seeks to make the results of this research\u00a0widely and easily accessible to people in the United States and India, indeed\u00a0throughout the world.

"}}]

fields.short_abstract: Sheet maps of Chicago from the 1860s, 1870s, and 1880s that are held at the University of Chicago Library's Map Collection.
fields.full_description:
[{"id": "c79d1539-5988-4737-b147-9517d4b7281c", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

Sheet maps of Chicago from the 1860s, 1870s, and 1880s that are held at the\u00a0University of Chicago Library's Map Collection. During these three decades,\u00a0Chicago grew from a small city of 109,000 into a large one with a population of\u00a0more than 1,000,000. It is often said that no city of the Western world had\u00a0ever grown so quickly. Chicago's growth was in part associated with its status\u00a0as the most important node in the American railroad system, which reached the\u00a0Pacific in 1869. Industries prospered, particularly those involving the\u00a0transformation of the raw materials of the West into products destined for the\u00a0East. The Union Stockyards (1865), the South Works steel mills (1875), and the\u00a0Pullman railway-car plant (early 1880s) were iconic examples. Growth was only\u00a0barely interrupted by the catastrophic fire of 1871 in which perhaps a quarter\u00a0of Chicago's dwellings and most of its business district were burned. The Fire\u00a0did force the city to establish a new building code and perhaps encouraged a\u00a0new self-consciousness about planning. The years after the Fire saw the\u00a0implementation of the city's \"boulevard\" system and the inauguration of parks\u00a0along the Lakefront of which Lincoln Park (institutionalized in 1864) is\u00a0perhaps the best known example.

"}}]

fields.full_description:
[{"id": "1a9b9939-766f-4d90-8506-8925848682a9", "type": "paragraph", "value": {"paragraph": "

The papers contain detailed information about the legal and fiscal affairs of the haciendas of Tlapanaloya (Tequixquiac?), Jalapaxco (Chalchicomula), Tepechichilco (Zempoala), and the ingenio of Tuxpango (Orizaba); many other haciendas and properties are mentioned cursorily. The confraternity papers are related to similar papers, also concerning haciendas and mortgages, in the Puebla, Mexico, Hospicia Records. The precise nature of the connection between the Puebla Papers and the confraternity records is not clear, but the documents in Box 1, folder 31 record a formal request by the confraternity for the transfer from Puebla to Mexico of papers relating to litigation involving the estate of the Torija family. Possibly other papers from Puebla eventually came into the hands of the confraternity. Religious organizations in Puebla were involved in the same fiscal activities as the confraternity, and it is possible that Puebla institutions and the Mexican confraternity occasionally held different mortgages on the same properties. The latest item in the confraternity collection is dated 1858.

"}}]
